importantModules.role: The fiber core every renderer shares: the work loop that schedules, renders and commits, every built-in hook, and the host config a third party supplies.
The published react package: the component and hook API, context and the JSX runtime entries, deliberately thin because a renderer does the real work.
The DOM renderer entry, with the host-specific work in react-dom-bindings.
The DOM half of the DOM renderer: the fiber host config, the synthetic event system and the DOM server code react-dom links against.
The server rendering core shared by the Flight and Fizz server bundlers.
The client side of the Flight protocol, turning a streaming React model back into elements for the react-server-dom packages.
Flight bindings for the DOM under Webpack: browser, edge and node client and server entries plus a bundler plugin and a node register hook.
The same Flight DOM bindings as the Webpack package, built for Turbopack; one of several bundler-specific Flight packages.
The cooperative scheduler: a priority min-heap that yields work back to the browser between units.
Feature flags and invariants imported by every package; the seam where build variants diverge.
The React Native host renderer, built on the same reconciler as the DOM renderer.
A renderer with no host environment, used by the team to test and debug fiber without a DOM attached.
The Fast Refresh runtime and Babel plugin that bundler authors wire up so editing a component keeps its state.
The published ESLint plugin that enforces the Rules of React, with its own code path analysis and flat-config presets.
The devtools implementation, shared by the browser extensions and the standalone shell.
The Chrome, Firefox and Edge extension builds that package the shared devtools UI for a browser.
A private webpack-served harness of sample apps that react-devtools-inline and react-devtools-shared are developed against, including the e2e and perf pages.
A backwards-compatible shim for useSyncExternalStore, so store libraries can subscribe on any React version that has hooks.
A renderer that produces plain JavaScript objects instead of DOM nodes; deprecated as of React 19 in favour of jsdom-based tests.
Private helpers the test suites depend on: the internal act implementation, console mocks and the jsdom setup.
The compiler's design notes in Markdown: its goals and architecture, the development guide, and the working notes and per-pass plans for the Rust port.
The compiler workspace: the Babel plugin that memoises component output, an ESLint plugin, the runtime, a healthcheck CLI, the snap runner and an editor server.
A Rust port of the compiler as react_compiler_* crates for AST, HIR, SSA, inference, optimization and validation, scored against the JS fixtures.
Scripts for the compiler workspace: npm release publishing, ESLint rule doc generation, HIR and error debug printers, and the Rust-versus-TypeScript port diffs.
The Rollup build: the bundle manifest, the per-release-channel builds, and the packaging and validation steps that produce npm tarballs.
The benchmark runner: it builds the local and merge-base bundles, serves four sample apps and measures each with Lighthouse, then prints both sets of timings.
The manual release path: build, check dependencies, prepare a build from CI and publish; most releases are prereleases shipped by CI instead.
The single source of truth for publishing: the React version, the canary channel label and the version of every stable package.

strengths: One reconciler, many renderers: DOM, native, server and test all sit on the same fiber core rather than forking it.
The public surface is deliberately thin; packages/react barely contains logic and defers to the reconciler.
Build variants (stable, experimental, www) are expressed as feature flags and separate index files rather than branches.
CI is split by area, so a compiler change and a runtime change do not have to run each other's suites.
Release, versioning and error-code tooling are checked in under scripts instead of living in a maintainer's shell history.
concerns: Two projects share one repository: compiler is a separate workspace with its own yarn.lock and packages, which doubles the tree a newcomer has to read.
packages holds around 40 packages and react-devtools-shared alone is larger than most of the runtime, so package count is a poor guide to importance.
The reconciler's meaning lives in a few very large files such as ReactFiberWorkLoop.js and ReactFiberHooks.js, which the directory layout does not signal.
Over 1,300 open issues and pull requests are attached to the repository, so the tracker is a firehose rather than a work queue.
